summary: Defines the Segment Routing Header (SRH), a new IPv6 routing extension header used to apply Segment Routing to the IPv6 data plane. It describes the header and how SR-capable nodes process it to steer packets along a list of segments.

plainLanguage.summary: A package carries a list of stops it must visit. This is the label on the package that holds that list and tells each stop where to send it next.

questions: what is the ipv6 segment routing header
what is the srh hmac tlv
subtitle: The IPv6 routing header that carries an ordered list of segments, so a packet can be steered hop by hop along a chosen path.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing steers a packet through a list of segments, but on the IPv6 data plane there needed to be a concrete place in the packet to carry that list and clear rules for nodes that handle it.
tldr.mechanism: The Segment Routing Header (SRH) is a new IPv6 Routing Extension Header, Routing Type 4, holding a Segment List of 128-bit addresses and a Segments Left counter. Each segment endpoint decrements the counter and copies the next segment into the IPv6 destination address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9800. It is meant for use inside a trusted SR domain, protected by ingress filtering and optionally by an HMAC TLV.

today: RFC 8754 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9800. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base definition of the SRH, and readers should also consult RFC 9800.

sections.title: Applying Segment Routing to IPv6
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) can run over two data planes, MPLS and IPv6, as described in RFC 8402. RFC 8754 defines how it is done for IPv6, using a new type of routing header called the Segment Routing Header (SRH). It also defines how SR-capable nodes use it.

The terms SR domain, SRv6, Segment Identifier (SID), Active Segment and SR Policy come from RFC 8402. In SRv6 a SID is an IPv6 address, so the segment currently being visited sits in the packet's destination address.

Three roles matter. An SR source node originates a packet with a segment in the destination address. A transit node forwards a packet whose destination is not one of its own segments or interfaces, and does not need to understand the SRH. An SR segment endpoint node receives a packet whose destination address is one of its local segments or interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: A trip with several stops needs a written itinerary. The source writes it, the stops follow it, and the roads in between simply carry the traveler along.

sections.title: The Segment Routing Header
sections.content:
The SRH is an IPv6 routing header with Routing Type 4. It starts with the usual Next Header, Hdr Ext Len, Routing Type and Segments Left fields from RFC 8200, followed by Last Entry, an 8-bit Flags field, a 16-bit Tag, the Segment List and optional TLVs.

Last Entry is the zero-based index of the last element of the Segment List. The Segment List is stored in reverse: Segment List[0] holds the last segment of the SR Policy, and the highest index holds the first. No flags are defined yet; they MUST be 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt. The Tag marks a packet as part of a class or group, and is set to zero when unused. How tags are allocated and used is out of scope.

Of the base fields, Segments Left is mutable while Next Header, Hdr Ext Len and Routing Type are not. Future SIDs MUST specify the mutability of Flags, Tag and Segment List.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a stack of address cards written back to front, with a pointer saying which card to read next.

sections.title: SRH TLVs: Padding and HMAC
sections.content:
After the Segment List the SRH can carry optional Type Length Value (TLV) objects. TLVs are present when Hdr Ext Len is greater than (Last Entry+1)*2. Unrecognized TLV types MUST be ignored, and the top bit of the type says whether the data can change en route. A TLV that runs past the end of the SRH causes an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, and the packet is discarded.

Two TLV kinds are defined. Pad1 (type 0) is a single byte of padding, and PadN (type 4) carries 0 to 5 bytes of zero padding; they align later TLVs and pad the SRH to a multiple of 8 octets. An implementation that adds or parses TLVs MUST support padding TLVs.

The optional HMAC TLV (type 5) lets a receiver verify that the SRH was chosen by an authorized party and that the Segment List was not changed after it was generated. It has a D bit, a 4-octet HMAC Key ID that names the pre-shared key and algorithm, and an HMAC of at most 32 octets. An implementation that supports HMAC MUST implement SHA-256 from SHA-2. If verification fails, an ICMP Parameter Problem SHOULD be sent (rate limited) and logged, and the packet SHOULD be discarded. Key selection and distribution are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: TLVs are sticky notes on the itinerary. Some are blank filler to keep things lined up, and one is a signature that proves the itinerary was not tampered with.

sections.title: How Nodes Process an SRH
sections.content:
An SR source node steers a packet into an SR Policy. If the policy has a single segment and nothing else needs to be added, the destination address is set to that segment and the SRH MAY be omitted. Otherwise the source sets Routing Type to 4, puts the first segment in the destination address, and sets both Segments Left and Last Entry to n-1, where n is the number of elements in the policy. A reduced SRH leaves out the first segment, which is already in the destination address, and sets Last Entry to n-2.

A transit node MUST NOT inspect the routing header and forwards the packet by its IPv6 routing table. At a segment endpoint, a longest-prefix match on the destination address decides what happens. For a locally instantiated SRv6 SID defined in this document, if Segments Left is zero the node moves on to the next header. Otherwise it decrements Segments Left, copies Segment List[Segments Left] into the destination address, decrements the Hop Limit and resubmits the packet. A bad Last Entry or Segments Left value triggers an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0. If the Hop Limit is 1 or less, an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent.

When the upper-layer header is IPv4 or IPv6 and local configuration permits, the endpoint decapsulates the packet. Otherwise it sends an ICMP Parameter Problem with the new code 4, "SR Upper-layer Header Error". A node whose matching FIB entry is only a local interface ignores the SRH if Segments Left is zero and discards the packet if it is not.
sections.plainLanguage: At each stop, the person crosses one place off the list, writes the next stop on the package, and sends it on. When the list is used up, the package is opened.

sections.title: Deployment Inside an SR Domain
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on using SIDs only inside the SR domain and only for packets of that domain, so the domain acts as one routing system. Nodes outside are not trusted and must not be able to use the domain's SIDs. Two layers of access lists enforce this: edge nodes drop packets arriving from outside with a destination address in the domain's SID block, and each internal node drops packets to its own SIDs whose source address is outside the domain. Failing to filter at the edge exposes the domain to the source-routing attacks described in RFC 5095.

The HMAC TLV supports delegation. A host can add an SRH that was computed elsewhere, and a trusted top-of-rack switch can verify the HMAC before the packet enters the network, so the host itself does not need to know the key.

Other operational rules: ingress nodes should expect encapsulation to affect the MTU, so a larger MTU inside the domain is RECOMMENDED. For ICMP errors, the SID at Segment List[0] may be used as the original destination. For load balancing, the source MUST set a flow label for interdomain packets and SHOULD do so for intradomain packets, and transit and endpoint nodes MUST use it in ECMP hashing as defined in RFC 6438. Other deployment models are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The itinerary only works inside a gated neighborhood. Guards at the gate tear up any outside note that tries to use the neighborhood's secret stop names.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC writes an SR Policy as <S1,S2,S3>, meaning S1 is visited first, and the same list as encoded in the SRH as (S3,S2,S1; SL), where SL is Segments Left. It then walks through an example topology. Host 8 sends a packet to host 9 using the policy <S7,A9>, which is sent as (A8,S7)(A9,S7; SL=1). Node 7 processes it and forwards (A8,A9)(A9,S7; SL=0).

For traffic entering from outside, the ingress router encapsulates the original packet in an outer IPv6 header with an SRH. The illustrations also cover the reduced variant and the case where a packet with a single-segment policy gets an outer header with no SRH at all.

The last example uses the HMAC TLV. An SDN controller gives host 8 an SRH with the list <S5,S7,S6,A9> and an HMAC. Node 5 is configured to require HMAC verification for packets destined to the domain's SID block, verifies it, and forwards the packet to the next segment.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a package hopping from stop to stop, with the little counter on it going down by one each time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security story rests on filtering. Packets entering the domain with a SID as destination must be dropped at the edge, each endpoint drops packets to its SIDs from outside the domain, and BCP 38 ingress filtering of source addresses SHOULD be used. Full protection blocks the attacks documented in RFC 5095 from outside the domain. Compromised nodes inside the domain can still mount attacks.

The SRH is unencrypted, so anyone able to snoop packets inside the domain may learn topology, flows and service usage, though the RFC notes an attacker there has other ways to learn that. ICMP generation could be abused for denial of service, which standard ICMPv6 rate limiting addresses. Because the SR domain is trusted, the RFC does not rely on the IP Authentication Header (AH) to secure the SRH, and leaves any use of SRH with AH to future documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The main protection is a strong gate. Notes from outsiders are thrown away, and inside the gate everyone is trusted, so the itinerary is not secret.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers Routing Type 4 for the Segment Routing Header and a new ICMPv6 Parameter Problem code 4, "SR Upper-layer Header Error". It creates two registries, "Segment Routing Header Flags" and "Segment Routing Header TLVs", both with the "IETF Review" procedure.

TLV codepoints 0 to 127 are for TLVs that do not change en route and 128 to 255 for those that may. Defined values are Pad1 (0), PadN (4) and HMAC (5). Values 1, 2, 3 and 6 are reserved for compatibility with early drafts, 124 to 126 and 252 to 254 are for experimentation and test, and 127 and 255 are reserved for expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers on the itinerary's labels are written in an official list so that nobody uses the same number for two different things.

fields.name: Segments Left
fields.desc: Index of the next segment to visit; mutable.

fields.name: Last Entry
fields.desc: Zero-based index of the last Segment List element.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: None defined; must be 0 on transmission.

fields.name: Tag
fields.desc: Marks a class or group of packets.

fields.name: Segment List[0..n]
fields.desc: 128-bit IPv6 addresses, stored with the last segment first.
